title: Gross Pay, Net Pay, Taxes & Deductions
summary: Learn how gross pay becomes net pay through applicable taxes, deductions, benefit contributions, and other payroll items.
objectives: Distinguish gross pay from net pay.
Identify common categories of payroll deductions.
Explain why deductions can vary by worker, employer, location, and benefit choices.

vocab.def: Earnings before applicable taxes and other deductions are subtracted.
Pay remaining after applicable deductions are subtracted.
Money an employer may withhold from pay for applicable taxes or other authorized purposes.
An amount subtracted from earnings for an applicable tax, benefit, contribution, or other authorized item.

sections.heading: Gross pay is not the same as take-home pay
sections.body: Gross pay describes earnings before applicable deductions. Net pay is the amount remaining after those deductions.

sections.heading: Different deductions have different purposes
sections.body: A pay statement may include tax withholding, benefit contributions, retirement contributions, or other authorized deductions depending on the worker and employer.

sections.heading: Payroll details can vary
sections.body: Tax rules, benefit choices, payroll practices, and deductions can differ by jurisdiction, employer, employment arrangement, and individual circumstances.

sections.heading: Use the right source when something is unclear
sections.body: For questions about a real paycheck, employees should use appropriate employer payroll or human-resources channels and qualified tax or financial professionals when individualized advice is needed.

practice.prompt: A worker earns $800 gross pay and receives $650 net pay. What should they review to understand the difference?
practice.answer: Review the listed deductions and withholding items on the pay statement.

practice.prompt: Do all workers have exactly the same deductions?
practice.answer: No. Deductions can vary based on applicable rules, employer plans, elections, and individual circumstances.

lab.objective: Use a simulated pay statement to identify gross pay, deductions, and net pay without using real learner payroll or tax information.

reflectionPrompt: Why is it risky to build a spending plan using gross pay instead of the money you actually receive?
